zh.q: 桌上这一串东西，哪一段在「造」气体，哪一段在「吃」气体？
zh.concl: 这就是教材「氮及其化合物」里的两个实验摆在一张台面上：一套是图5-14 的「硝酸与铜反应」（两支具支试管 + 尾气 NaOH），一个是图5-10 的「二氧化氮溶于水」（注射器）。
points: 从左到右就是操作顺序：先让金属与硝酸接触产生气体 → 尾气吸收 → 把无色气体收进注射器做转化实验。
两支试管是同高的对照：左管始终是「铜 + 浓硝酸」，右管才是被改的那一支；注射器里的那 20 mL 气体就是从这套装置收来的。
教材图5-14 的两支试管本来就是「浓一支、稀一支，观察并比较」；本课把左管固定成基准管、右管随工况变，这样每一步都有对照。

zh.q: 铜丝一插进浓硝酸，为什么马上冒出红棕色气体？
zh.concl: 硝酸是很强的氧化剂：它把铜氧化成 Cu²⁺，自身被还原成 NO₂（N 由 +5 降到 +4，每个 N 得 1 个电子）；NO₂ 是红棕色气体。教材用「向上拉铜丝」来随时终止反应。
points: 硝酸与金属反应不放氢气（放 H₂ 的是稀硫酸、盐酸那一路）；浓硝酸的还原产物是 NO₂，N 由 +5 降到 +4。
红棕色是 NO₂ 的颜色，NO 是无色的；两种气体都无色无味地记混，是这课最常见的错误。
教材练习第 6 题原文说浓硝酸这一支「反应剧烈进行，铜丝逐渐变细，溶液变绿，试管上方出现红棕色气体」——变绿不是铜离子变色：NO₂ 溶在酸里显黄、Cu²⁺ 显蓝，两层叠起来才是绿色。

zh.q: 换成稀硝酸，气体怎么变成无色了？它跑到哪去了？
zh.concl: 稀硝酸的氧化性比浓硝酸弱：N 只被还原到 +2，产物是无色、难溶于水的 NO（每个 N 得 3 个电子）。NO 一接触空气里的氧气就立刻变成红棕色的 NO₂（2NO + O₂ = 2NO₂）——所以「无色」只是暂时的。
points: 浓、稀硝酸的还原产物不同（NO₂ / NO），但都不是氢气：N 分别被还原到 +4 和 +2。
稀硝酸实验中「试管中的气体略有红棕色」是 NO 被空气里的氧气氧化了，不是稀硝酸本来产生红棕色气体（教材练习第 6 题原题）。
同样多的铜，稀硝酸放出的气体物质的量只有浓硝酸的 1/3：1 mol Cu 失 2 mol 电子，浓硝酸得 2 mol NO₂、稀硝酸得 2/3 mol NO。

zh.q: 同一片铁片放进浓硝酸，怎么连气泡都没有了？
zh.concl: 常温下铁、铝的表面被浓硝酸氧化，生成一层致密薄膜把内部金属盖住（钝化），反应很快就停——所以能用铁制、铝制容器盛装浓硝酸；但同一片铁放进稀硝酸里照样反应。
points: 钝化不是「铁不与硝酸反应」，而是表面被浓硝酸氧化出一层致密薄膜，把内部金属盖住、阻止继续反应。
判据是气泡：钝化和铁遇稀硝酸这两格的 φ 都是 0.0 %，光看 φ 分不出来，必须看「反应快慢」这一格。
两个条件缺一不可：常温 + 浓硝酸。同一片铁片放进稀硝酸里照样持续冒泡（教材原话：铁、铝「虽然能与稀硝酸或稀硫酸反应」）。

zh.q: 这股红棕色气体要是直接排到屋里，会怎样？
zh.concl: NO 和 NO₂ 都是有毒气体。教材图5-14 右边那只烧杯里装的就是 NaOH 溶液、导管末端浸在液面以下，用来把尾气吸收掉；接不接尾气只影响安全和环境，不改变你制得了多少气体。
points: 尾气开关是安全开关：接不接它，主读数一格都不变（对照第 2 步的 100.0 %）。
导管要浸到液面以下才算「吸收」，悬在液面上方等于直排。
教材没有给 NOx 与 NaOH 反应的方程式，本课也不写，只照图5-14 的图注说「用 NaOH 溶液吸收」。

zh.q: 浓硝酸为什么非得装在棕色瓶里、还得放阴凉处？
zh.concl: 浓硝酸见光或受热会分解：4HNO₃ = 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ + 2H₂O，放出的 NO₂ 把酸染黄、把瓶内压力顶高，所以必须盛在棕色试剂瓶里、放在阴凉处——这也是教材练习第 6(1) 题的答案。
points: 分解产物里有 NO₂，所以「看见红棕色」本身就说明酸已经在分解。
不只避光：受热一样分解，所以还要放阴凉处。
这是保存问题不是反应问题：换掉瓶子，试管里的反应一点都不变。

zh.q: 无色的 NO 吸进 10 mL 空气，怎么立刻变红了？
zh.concl: 空气里只有约 21 % 的氧气：吸 10 mL 空气只带进 2.1 mL O₂，只够把 4.2 mL NO 氧化成 NO₂（2NO + O₂ = 2NO₂），所以颜色深浅取决于吸了多少空气，剩下的 NO 还是无色。
points: 决定颜色的是「吸进来的氧气有多少」，不是「吸了几口」：每 10 mL 空气只带 2.1 mL O₂。
一次吸 10 mL 空气远不够把 20 mL NO 全部转化——教材思考题问的就是这件事。
注射器只有 50 mL，最多吸到第 3 轮，所以要让 NO 充分转化必须反复吸、反复振荡。

zh.q: 摇一摇注射器，红棕色为什么褪了、活塞为什么往里缩？
zh.concl: NO₂ 溶于水时发生歧化：3NO₂ + H₂O = 2HNO₃ + NO，3 个 N 里 2 个升到 +5、1 个降到 +2——所以 NO₂ 既是氧化剂又是还原剂；每 3 体积 NO₂ 只留下 1 体积 NO，气体少了 2/3，活塞就往里缩。
points: NO₂ 溶于水不是「被水吸住不动」，而是歧化：一部分变成硝酸、一部分又变回 NO。
所以吸收不彻底：每 3 mol NO₂ 只得到 2 mol 硝酸，另 1 mol 变回 NO——工业上要补空气再氧化（课标情境素材「工业制硝酸」）。
每轮活塞内缩 2.8 mL 正好等于那一轮被吸收 NO₂ 体积的 2/3（4.2 × 2/3）。

zh.q: 考核：把注射器里的 NO 尽量转化成硝酸，同时守住两条安全线
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：NO 要反复通空气并振荡才能转化得多；尾气不接收、硝酸不避光，实验做得再漂亮也是不合格。
points: 只吸空气不振荡：红棕色越积越深、φ 一路涨到 28.8 %，永远达不到 0.0 %。
少吸一轮就差一截：每轮振荡后 NO 只减少 2.8 mL（20 → 17.2 → 14.4 mL）。
尾气被拔掉是唯一会「把分扣回来」的异常，别只盯着读数。

en.q: Of this row of equipment on the bench, which part "makes" gas and which part "consumes" it?
en.concl: These are two experiments from the textbook's "Nitrogen and Its Compounds" on one bench: Fig. 5-14, "nitric acid reacting with copper" (two side-arm test tubes + NaOH for tail gas), and Fig. 5-10, "nitrogen dioxide dissolving in water" (syringe).
points: Left to right is the order of operations: bring metal and nitric acid together to make gas → absorb the tail gas → draw the colorless gas into the syringe for the conversion experiment.
The two test tubes are a matched control: the left is always "copper + concentrated nitric acid", and only the right one is changed; the 20 mL of gas in the syringe was collected from this setup.

The two tubes in textbook Fig. 5-14 were meant as "one concentrated, one dilute, observe and compare"; this lesson fixes the left tube as the baseline and lets the right one vary, so every step has a control.

en.q: Why does red-brown gas appear the moment the copper wire goes into concentrated nitric acid?
en.concl: Nitric acid is a strong oxidizer: it oxidizes copper to Cu²⁺ and is itself reduced to NO₂ (N from +5 to +4, each N gaining 1 electron); NO₂ is a red-brown gas. The textbook uses "pull up the copper wire" to stop the reaction at any time.
points: Nitric acid reacting with metals doesn't release hydrogen (that's dilute sulfuric and hydrochloric acid); the reduction product of concentrated nitric acid is NO₂, with N going from +5 to +4.
Red-brown is the color of NO₂; NO is colorless. Mixing up which gas is colorless is the most common mistake in this lesson.

Textbook exercise 6 says that for concentrated nitric acid "the reaction is vigorous, the copper wire gradually thins, the solution turns green, and red-brown gas appears above"; the green isn't copper ions changing color: NO₂ dissolved in the acid looks yellow and Cu²⁺ looks blue, and together they look green.

en.q: With dilute nitric acid, why does the gas become colorless? Where did the color go?
en.concl: Dilute nitric acid is a weaker oxidizer than concentrated: N is only reduced to +2, giving colorless NO that is barely soluble in water (each N gains 3 electrons). As soon as NO touches oxygen in the air it becomes red-brown NO₂ (2NO + O₂ = 2NO₂), so "colorless" is only temporary.
points: Concentrated and dilute nitric acid give different reduction products (NO₂ / NO), but neither gives hydrogen: N is reduced to +4 and +2 respectively.
"The gas in the tube is slightly red-brown" in the dilute nitric acid experiment is NO being oxidized by oxygen in the air, not dilute nitric acid producing red-brown gas (textbook exercise 6).

For the same amount of copper, dilute nitric acid releases only 1/3 as many moles of gas as concentrated: 1 mol Cu gives up 2 mol electrons, which makes 2 mol NO₂ with concentrated acid but 2/3 mol NO with dilute.

en.q: Put an iron strip into concentrated nitric acid. Why are there no bubbles at all?
en.concl: At room temperature the surfaces of iron and aluminum are oxidized by concentrated nitric acid into a dense film that covers the metal inside (passivation), and the reaction soon stops, so iron and aluminum containers can hold concentrated nitric acid; but the same iron reacts in dilute nitric acid.
points: Passivation isn't "iron doesn't react with nitric acid"; the surface is oxidized by concentrated nitric acid into a dense film that covers the metal inside and stops further reaction.
Bubbles are the test: passivation and iron in dilute nitric acid both show φ = 0.0 %, so φ alone can't tell them apart; you must look at "reaction rate".

Both conditions are needed: room temperature + concentrated nitric acid. The same iron strip bubbles steadily in dilute nitric acid (textbook: iron and aluminum "although they can react with dilute nitric or dilute sulfuric acid").

en.q: 这股红棕色气体要是直接排到屋里，会怎样？
en.concl: NO and NO₂ are both toxic gases. The beaker on the right of textbook Fig. 5-14 holds NaOH solution with the tube end below the surface to absorb the tail gas; connecting it only affects safety and the environment, not how much gas you make.
points: The tail gas switch is a safety switch: connected or not, the main reading doesn't change at all (compare the 100.0 % in step 2).
The tube must be below the surface to count as "absorbing"; hanging above the surface is the same as venting straight out.
The textbook doesn't give the equation for NOx with NaOH, and this lesson doesn't either; it only follows the caption of Fig. 5-14, "absorb with NaOH solution".

en.q: Why must concentrated nitric acid be kept in a brown bottle, and in a cool place?
en.concl: Concentrated nitric acid decomposes in light or when heated: 4HNO₃ = 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ + 2H₂O. The NO₂ released turns the acid yellow and raises the pressure in the bottle, so it must be kept in a brown reagent bottle in a cool place. This is also the answer to textbook exercise 6(1).
points: The decomposition products include NO₂, so "seeing red-brown" itself shows the acid is decomposing.
Not just light: heat decomposes it too, so it also needs a cool place.
This is a storage issue, not a reaction issue: change the bottle and the reaction in the test tube doesn't change at all.

en.q: Draw 10 mL of air into the colorless NO. Why does it turn red at once?
en.concl: Air is only about 21 % oxygen: drawing in 10 mL of air brings just 2.1 mL of O₂, enough to oxidize only 4.2 mL of NO to NO₂ (2NO + O₂ = 2NO₂). So how deep the color gets depends on how much air you draw in, and the remaining NO stays colorless.
points: What sets the color is "how much oxygen is drawn in", not "how many draws": each 10 mL of air brings only 2.1 mL of O₂.
One 10 mL draw of air is far from enough to convert all 20 mL of NO; this is exactly what the textbook's thinking question asks.
The syringe is only 50 mL, so you can draw at most 3 rounds; to convert NO fully you must draw and shake repeatedly.

en.q: Shake the syringe. Why does the red-brown fade and the plunger move in?
en.concl: NO₂ disproportionates when it dissolves in water: 3NO₂ + H₂O = 2HNO₃ + NO; of 3 N atoms, 2 rise to +5 and 1 falls to +2, so NO₂ is both oxidizer and reducer; every 3 volumes of NO₂ leave just 1 volume of NO, so the gas shrinks by 2/3 and the plunger moves in.
points: NO₂ dissolving in water isn't "held by the water"; it disproportionates: some becomes nitric acid and some turns back into NO.

So absorption is incomplete: every 3 mol of NO₂ gives only 2 mol of nitric acid, while 1 mol turns back into NO; industry has to add more air to reoxidize it (curriculum context "industrial nitric acid production").
Each round the plunger moves in 2.8 mL, exactly 2/3 of the NO₂ volume absorbed that round (4.2 × 2/3).

en.q: Assessment: convert as much of the NO in the syringe to nitric acid as possible, while holding both safety lines
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: NO only converts well with repeated air and shaking; if the tail gas isn't absorbed or the acid isn't kept dark, the experiment fails however nice it looks.
points: Drawing in air without shaking: the red-brown keeps building and φ climbs to 28.8 %, never reaching 0.0 %.
One round short leaves a gap: each shake only reduces NO by 2.8 mL (20 → 17.2 → 14.4 mL).
The tail gas being disconnected is the only fault that "takes points back", so don't watch only the reading.
